entries.712c945a68be2f18bf292459476152c161dad290: <div sID="gen5762" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="24" osisID="1Sam.24" sID="1Sam.24"/> <div eID="gen5762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5763" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5764" type="x-p"/> We have hitherto had Saul seeking an opportunity to destroy David, and, to his shame, he could never find it. In this chapter David had a fair opportunity to destroy Saul, and, to his honour, he did not make use of it; and his sparing Saul's life was as great an instance of God's grace in him as the preserving of his own life was of God's providence over him. Observe, I. How maliciously Saul sought David's life, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.1-1Sam.24.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. How generously David saved Saul's life (when he had him at an advantage) and only cut off the skirt of his robe, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.3-1Sam.24.8">ver. 3-8</reference>. III. How pathetically he reasoned with Saul, upon this to bring him to a better temper towards him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.9-1Sam.24.15">ver. 9-15</reference>. IV. The good impression this made upon Saul for the present, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.16-1Sam.24.22">ver. 16-22</reference>.
entries.4ab36dc420390437f344753bea3563594497ce5d: <div eID="gen5764" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5763" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David Spares Saul in the Cave. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5765" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass, when Saul was returned from following the Philistines, that it was told him, saying, Behold, David <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the wilderness of Engedi. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then Saul took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel, and went to seek David and his men upon the rocks of the wild goats. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he came to the sheepcotes by the way, where <hi type="italic">was</hi> a cave; and Saul went in to cover his feet: and David and his men remained in the sides of the cave. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the men of David said unto him, Behold the day of which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand, that thou mayest do to him as it shall seem good unto thee. Then David arose, and cut off the skirt of Saul's robe privily. <hi type="super">5</hi> And it came to pass afterward, that David's heart smote him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt. <hi type="super">6</hi> And he said unto his men, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he <hi type="italic">is</hi> the anointed of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">7</hi> So David stayed his servants with these words, and suffered them not to rise against Saul. But Saul rose up out of the cave, and went on <hi type="italic">his</hi> way. <hi type="super">8</hi> David also arose afterward, and went out of the cave, and cried after Saul, saying, My lord the king. And when Saul looked behind him, David stooped with his face to the earth, and bowed himself. <div eID="gen5765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5766" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Saul renews his pursuit of David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.1-1Sam.24.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. No sooner had he come home safely from chasing the Philistines, in which it should seem he had good success, than he enquired after David to do him a mischief, and resolved to have another thrust at him, <hi type="italic">as if he had been delivered to do all these abominations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.7.10">Jer. vii. 10</reference>. By the frequent incursions of the Philistines, he might have seen how necessary it was to recall David from his banishment and restore him to his place in the army again; but so far is he from doing this that now more than ever he is exasperated against him, and, hearing that he is <hi type="italic">in the wilderness of En-gedi,</hi> he draws out 3000 choice men, and goes with them at his feet in pursuit of him <hi type="italic">upon the rocks of the wild goats,</hi> where, one would think, David should not have been envied a habitation nor Saul desirous of disturbing him; for what harm could he fear from one who was no better accommodated? But it is not enough for Saul that David is thus cooped up; he cannot be easy while he is alive. <div eID="gen5766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5767" type="x-p"/> II. Providence brings Saul alone into the same cave wherein David and his men had hidden themselves, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.3">v. 3</reference>. In those countries there were very large caves in the sides of the rocks or mountains, partly natural, but probably much enlarged by art for the sheltering of sheep from the heat of the sun; hence we read of places where the flocks did rest at noon (<reference osisRef="Song.1.7">Cant. i. 7</reference>), and this cave seems to be spoken of as one of the sheep-cotes. In the sides of this cave David and his men remained, perhaps not all his men, the whole 600, but only some few of his particular friends, the rest being disposed of in similar retirements. Saul, passing by, turned in himself alone, not in search of David (for, supposing him to be an aspiring ambitious man, he thought to find him rather climbing with the wild goats upon the rocks than retiring with the sheep into a cave), but thither he turned aside to <hi type="italic">cover his feet,</hi> that is, to sleep awhile, it being a cool and quiet place, and very refreshing in the heat of the day; probably he ordered his attendants to march before, reserving only a very few to wait for him at the mouth of the cave. Some by the covering of the feet understand the easing of nature, and think that this was Saul's errand into the cave: but the former interpretation is more probable. <div eID="gen5767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5768" type="x-p"/> III. David's servants stir him up to kill Saul now that he has so fair an opportunity to do it, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.4">v. 4</reference>. They reminded him that this was the day which he had long looked for, and of which God had spoken to him in general when he was anointed to the kingdom, which should put a period to his troubles and open the passage to his advancement. Saul now lay at his mercy, and it was easy to imagine how little mercy he would find with Saul and therefore what little reason he had to show mercy to him. "By all means" (say his servants) "give him the fatal blow now." See how apt we are to misunderstand, 1. The promises of God. God had assured David that he would deliver him from Saul, and his men interpret this as a warrant to destroy Saul. 2. The providences of God. Because it was now in his power to kill him, they concluded he might lawfully do it. <div eID="gen5768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5769" type="x-p"/> IV. David <hi type="italic">cut off the skirt of his robe,</hi> but soon repented that he had done this: <hi type="italic">His heart smote him</hi> for it (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.5">v. 5</reference>); though it did Saul no real hurt, and served David for a proof that it was in his power to have killed him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.11">v. 11</reference>), yet, because it was an affront to Saul's royal dignity, he wished he had not done it. Note, It is a good thing to have a heart within us smiting us for sins that seem little; it is a sign that conscience is awake and tender, and will be the means of preventing greater sins. <div eID="gen5769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5770" type="x-p"/> V. He reasons strongly both with himself and with his servants against doing Saul any hurt. 1. He reasons with himself (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord forbid that I should do this thing.</hi> Note, Sin is a thing which it becomes us to startle at, and to resist the temptations to, not only with resolution, but with a holy indignation. He considered Saul now, not as his enemy, and the only person that stood in the way of his preferment (for then he would be induced to hearken to the temptation), but as God's anointed (that is, the person whom God had appointed to reign as long as he lived, and who, as such, was under the particular protection of the divine law), and as his master, to whom he was obliged to be faithful. Let servants and subjects learn hence to be dutiful and loyal, whatever hardships are put upon them, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.18">1 Pet. ii. 18</reference>. 2. He reasons with his servants: <hi type="italic">He suffered them not to rise against Saul,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.7">v. 7</reference>. He would not only not do this evil thing himself, but he would not suffer those about him to do it. Thus did he render good for evil to him from whom he had received evil for good, and was herein both a type of Christ, who saved his persecutors, and an example to all Christians not to be <hi type="italic">overcome of evil, but to overcome evil with good.</hi> <div eID="gen5770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5771" type="x-p"/> VI. He followed Saul out of the cave, and, though he would not take the opportunity to slay him, yet he wisely took the opportunity, if possible, to slay his enmity, by convincing him that he was not such a man as he took him for. 1. Even in showing his head now he testified that he had an honourable opinion of Saul. He had too much reason to believe that, let him say what he would, Saul would immediately be the death of him as soon as he saw him, and yet he bravely lays aside that jealousy, and thinks Saul so much a man of sense as to hear his reasoning when he had so much to say in his own vindication and such fresh and sensible proofs to give of his own integrity. 2. His behaviour was very respectful: He <hi type="italic">stooped with his face to the earth, and bowed himself,</hi> giving honour to whom honour was due, and teaching us to order ourselves lowly and reverently to all our superiors, even to those that have been most injurious to us.
entries.af026a6e4366128a657cf782831b4539b9b8d622: <div eID="gen5771" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Expostulates with Saul. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5772" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And David said to Saul, Wherefore hearest thou men's words, saying, Behold, David seeketh thy hurt? <hi type="super">10</hi> Behold, this day thine eyes have seen how that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had delivered thee to day into mine hand in the cave: and <hi type="italic">some</hi> bade <hi type="italic">me</hi> kill thee: but <hi type="italic">mine eye</hi> spared thee; and I said, I will not put forth mine hand against my lord; for he <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's anointed. <hi type="super">11</hi> Moreover, my father, see, yea, see the skirt of thy robe in my hand: for in that I cut off the skirt of thy robe, and killed thee not, know thou and see that <hi type="italic">there is</hi> neither evil nor transgression in mine hand, and I have not sinned against thee; yet thou huntest my soul to take it. <hi type="super">12</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> judge between me and thee, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> avenge me of thee: but mine hand shall not be upon thee. <hi type="super">13</hi> As saith the proverb of the ancients, Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked: but mine hand shall not be upon thee. <hi type="super">14</hi> After whom is the king of Israel come out? after whom dost thou pursue? after a dead dog, after a flea. <hi type="super">15</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> therefore be judge, and judge between me and thee, and see, and plead my cause, and deliver me out of thine hand. <div eID="gen5772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5773" type="x-p"/> We have here David's warm and pathetic speech to Saul, wherein he endeavours to convince him that he did him a great deal of wrong in persecuting him thus and to persuade him therefore to be reconciled. <div eID="gen5773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5774" type="x-p"/> I. He calls him <hi type="italic">father</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.11">v. 11</reference>), for he was not only, as king, the father of his country, but he was, in particular, his father-in-law. From a father one may expect compassion and a favourable opinion. For a prince to seek the ruin of any of his good subjects is as unnatural as for a father to seek the ruin of his own children. <div eID="gen5774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5775" type="x-p"/> II. He lays the blame of his rage against him upon his evil counsellors: <hi type="italic">Wherefore hearest thou men's words?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.9">v. 9</reference>. It is a piece of respect due to crowned heads, if they do amiss, to charge it upon those about them, who either advised them to it or should have advised them against it. David had reason enough to think that Saul persecuted him purely from his own envy and malice, yet he courteously supposes that others put him on to do it, and made him believe that David was his enemy and sought his hurt. Satan, the great accuser of the brethren, has his agents in all places, and particularly in the courts of those princes that encourage them and give ear to them, who make it their business to represent the people of God as enemies to Caesar and hurtful to kings and provinces, that, being thus dressed up in bear-skins, they may "be baited." <div eID="gen5775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5776" type="x-p"/> III. He solemnly protests his own innocence, and that he is far from designing any hurt or mischief to Saul: "<hi type="italic">There is neither evil nor transgression in my hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.11">v. 11</reference>. I am not chargeable with any crime, nor conscious of any guilt, and, had I a window in my breast, thou mightest through it see the sincerity of my heart in this protestation: <hi type="italic">I have not sinned against thee</hi> (however I have sinned against God), <hi type="italic">yet thou huntest my soul,</hi>" that is, "my life." Perhaps it was about this time that David penned the seventh psalm, concerning the affair of Cush the Benjamite (that is, Saul, as some think), wherein he thus appeals to God (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.3-1Sam.24.5">v. 3-5</reference>): <hi type="italic">If there be iniquity in my hands, then let the enemy persecute my soul and take it,</hi> putting in a parenthesis, with reference to the story of this chapter, <hi type="italic">Yea, I have delivered him that without cause is my enemy.</hi> <div eID="gen5776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5777" type="x-p"/> IV. He produces undeniable evidence to prove the falsehood of the suggestion upon which Saul's malice against him was grounded. David was charged with seeking Saul's hurt: "<hi type="italic">See,</hi>" says he, "<hi type="italic">yea, see the skirt of thy robe,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.11">v. 11</reference>. Let this be a witness for me, and an unexceptionable witness it is; had that been true of which I am accused, I should now have had thy head in my hand and not the skirt of thy robe, for I could as easily have cut off that as this." To corroborate this evidence he shows him, 1. That God's providence had given him opportunity to do it: <hi type="italic">The lord delivered thee,</hi> very surprisingly, <hi type="italic">to day into my hand,</hi> whence many a one would have gathered an intimation that it was the will of God he should now give the determining blow to him whose neck lay so fair for it. When Saul had but a very small advantage against David he cried out, <hi type="italic">God has delivered him into my hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.7">ch. xxiii. 7</reference>), and resolved to make the best of that advantage; but David did not so. 2. That his counsellors and those about him had earnestly besought him to do it: <hi type="italic">Some bade me kill thee.</hi> He had blamed Saul for hearkening to men's words and justly; "for," says he, "if I had done so, thou wouldest not have been alive now." 3. That it was upon a good principle that he refused to do it; not because Saul's attendants were at hand, who, it may be, would have avenged his death; no, it was not by the fear of them, but by the fear of God, that he was restrained from it. "He is my lord, and the Lord's anointed, whom I ought to protect, and to whom I owe faith and allegiance, and therefore I said, I will not touch a hair of his head." Such a happy command he had of himself that his nature, in the midst of the greatest provocation, was not suffered to rebel against his principles. <div eID="gen5777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5778" type="x-p"/> V. He declares it to be his fixed resolution never to be his own avenger: "<hi type="italic">The Lord avenge me of thee,</hi> that is, deliver me out of thy hand; but, whatever comes of it, <hi type="italic">my hand shall not be upon thee</hi>" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.12">v. 12</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.13">v. 13</reference>), for <hi type="italic">saith the proverb of the ancients, Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked.</hi> The wisdom of the ancients is transmitted to posterity by their proverbial sayings. Many such we receive by tradition from our fathers; and the counsels of common persons are very much directed by this, "As the old saying is." Here is one that was in use in David's time: <hi type="italic">Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked,</hi> that is, 1. Men's own iniquity will ruin them at last, so some understand it. Forward furious men will cut their own throats with their own knives. Give them rope enough, and they will hang themselves. In this sense it comes in very fitly as a reason why <hi type="italic">his hand should not be upon him.</hi> 2. Bad men will do bad things; according as men's principles and dispositions are, so will their actions be. This also agrees very well with the connexion. If David had been a wicked man, as he was represented, he would have done this wicked thing; but he durst not, because of the fear of God. Or thus: Whatever injuries bad men do us (which we are not to wonder at; he that lies among thorns must expect to be scratched), yet we must not return them; never render railing for railing. Though <hi type="italic">wickedness proceed from the wicked,</hi> yet let it not therefore proceed from us by way of retaliation. Though the dog bark at the sheep, the sheep does not bark at the dog. See <reference osisRef="Isa.32.6-Isa.32.8">Isa. xxxii. 6-8</reference>. <div eID="gen5778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5779" type="x-p"/> VI. He endeavours to convince Saul that as it was a bad thing, so it was a mean thing, for him to give chase to such an inconsiderable person as he was (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whom does the king of Israel pursue</hi> with all this care and force? <hi type="italic">A dead dog; a flea; one flea,</hi> so it is in the Hebrew. It is below so great a king to enter the lists with one that is so unequal a match for him, one of his own servants, bred a poor shepherd, now an exile, neither able nor willing to make any resistance. To conquer him would not be to his honour, to attempt it was his disparagement. If Saul would consult his own reputation, he would slight such an enemy (supposing he were really his enemy) and would think himself in no danger from him. David was so far from aspiring that he was, in his own account, as a dead dog. Mephibosheth thus calls himself, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.8">2 Sam. ix. 8</reference>. This humble language would have wrought upon Saul if he had had any spark of generosity in him. <hi type="italic">Satis est prostrasse leoni—Enough for the lion that he has laid his victim low.</hi> What credit would it be to Saul to trample upon a dead dog? What pleasure could it be to him to hunt a flea, a single flea, which (as some have observed), if it be sought, is not easily found, if it be found, is not easily caught, and, if it be caught, is a poor prize, especially for a prince. <hi type="italic">Aquila non captat muscas—The eagle does not dart upon flies.</hi> David thinks Saul had no more reason to fear him than to fear a flea-bite. <div eID="gen5779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5780" type="x-p"/> VII. He once and again appeals to God as the righteous Judge (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.12">v. 12</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord judge between me and thee.</hi> Note, The justice of God is the refuge and comfort of oppressed innocence. If men wrong us, God will right us, at furthest, in the judgment of the great day. With him David leaves his cause, and so rests satisfied, waiting his time to appear for him.
entries.2f2e62777956042b2a583212247ac1d7e91efd1c: <div eID="gen5780" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Saul Relents at David's Reproof. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5781" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And it came to pass, when David had made an end of speaking these words unto Saul, that Saul said, <hi type="italic">Is</hi> this thy voice, my son David? And Saul lifted up his voice, and wept. <hi type="super">17</hi> And he said to David, Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> more righteous than I: for thou hast rewarded me good, whereas I have rewarded thee evil. <hi type="super">18</hi> And thou hast shewed this day how that thou hast dealt well with me: forasmuch as when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had delivered me into thine hand, thou killedst me not. <hi type="super">19</hi> For if a man find his enemy, will he let him go well away? wherefore the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> reward thee good for that thou hast done unto me this day. <hi type="super">20</hi> And now, behold, I know well that thou shalt surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in thine hand. <hi type="super">21</hi> Swear now therefore unto me by the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that thou wilt not cut off my seed after me, and that thou wilt not destroy my name out of my father's house. <hi type="super">22</hi> And David sware unto Saul. And Saul went home; but David and his men gat them up unto the hold. <div eID="gen5781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5782" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen5782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5783" type="x-p"/> I. Saul's penitent reply to David's speech. It was strange that he had patience to hear him out, considering how outrageous he was against him, and how cutting David's discourse was. But God restrained him and his men; and we may suppose Saul struck with amazement at the singularity of the event, and much more when he found how much he had lain at David's mercy. His heart must have been harder than a stone if this had not affected him. 1. He melted into tears, and we will not suppose them to have been counterfeit but real expressions of his present concern at the sight of his own iniquity, so plainly proved upon him. He speaks as one quite overcome with David's kindness: <hi type="italic">Is this thy voice, my son David?</hi> And, as one that relented at the thought of his own folly and ingratitude, he <hi type="italic">lifted up his voice and wept,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.16">v. 16</reference>. Many mourn for their sins that do not truly repent of them, weep bitterly for them, and yet continue in love and league with them. 2. He ingenuously acknowledges David's integrity and his own iniquity (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou art more righteous than I.</hi> Now God made good to David that word on which he had caused him to hope, that he would <hi type="italic">bring forth his righteousness as the light,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.6">Ps. xxxvii. 6</reference>. Those who take care to keep a good conscience may leave it to God to secure them the credit of it. This fair confession was enough to prove David innocent (even his enemy himself being judge), but not enough to prove Saul himself a true penitent. He should have said, <hi type="italic">Thou are righteous, but I am wicked;</hi> but the utmost he will own is this: <hi type="italic">Thou art more righteous than I.</hi> Bad men will commonly go no further than this in their confessions; they will own they are not so good as some others are; there are those that are better than they, and more righteous. He now owns himself under a mistake concerning David (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast shown this day</hi> that thou art so far from seeking my hurt <hi type="italic">that thou hast dealt well with me.</hi>" We are too apt to suspect others to be worse affected towards us then really they are, and than perhaps they are proved to be; and when, afterwards, our mistake is discovered, we should be forward to recall our suspicions, as Saul does here. 3. He prays God to recompense David for this his generous kindness to him. He owns that David's sparing him, when he had him in his power, was an uncommon and unparalleled instance of tenderness to an enemy; no man would have done the like; and therefore, either because he thought himself not able to give him a full recompence for so great a favour, or because he found himself not inclined to give him any recompence at all, he turns him over to God for his pay: <hi type="italic">The Lord reward thee good,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.19">v. 19</reference>. Poor beggars can do no less than pray for their benefactors, and Saul did no more. 4. He prophesies his advancement to the throne (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.20">v. 20</reference>): I <hi type="italic">know well that thou shalt surely be king.</hi> He knew it before, by the promise Samuel had made him of it compared with the excellent spirit that appeared in David, which highly aggravated his sin and folly in persecuting him as he did; he had as much reason to say concerning David as David concerning him, <hi type="italic">How can I put forth my hand against the Lord's anointed?</hi> But now he knew it by the interest he found David had in the people, the special providence of God in protecting him, and the generous kingly spirit he had now given a proof of in sparing his enemy. Now he knew it, that is, now that he was in a good temper he was willing to own that he knew it and to submit to the conviction of it. Note, Sooner or later, God will force even those that are of the synagogue of Satan to know and own those that he has loved, and to worship before their feet; for so is the promise, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Rev. iii. 9</reference>. This acknowledgement which Saul made of David's incontestable title to the crown was a great encouragement to David himself and a support to his faith and hope. 5. He binds David with an oath hereafter to show the same tenderness of his seed and of his name as he had now shown of his person, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.21">v. 21</reference>. David had more reason to oblige Saul by an oath that he would not destroy him, yet he insists not on that (if the laws of justice and honour would not bind him, an oath would not), but Saul knew David to be a conscientious man, and would think his interests safe if he could get them secured by his oath. Saul by his disobedience had ruined his own soul, and never took care by repentance to prevent that ruin, and yet is very solicitous that his name might not be destroyed nor his seed cut off. However, <hi type="italic">David swore unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.22">v. 22</reference>. Though he might be tempted, not only in revenge, but in prudence, to extirpate Saul's family, yet he binds himself not to do it, knowing that God could and would establish the kingdom to him and his, without the use of such bloody methods. This oath he afterwards religiously observed; he supported Mephibosheth, and executed those as traitors that slew Ishbosheth. The hanging up of seven of Saul's posterity, to atone for the destruction of the Gibeonites, was God's appointment, not David's act, and therefore not the violation of this oath. <div eID="gen5783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5784" type="x-p"/> II. Their parting in peace. 1. Saul, for the present, desisted from the persecution. He went home convinced, but not converted; ashamed of his envy of David, yet retaining in his breast that root of bitterness; vexed that, when at last he had found David, he could not at that time find in his heart to destroy him, as he had designed. God has many ways to tie the hands of persecutors, when he does not turn their hearts. 2. David continued to shift for his own safety. He knew Saul too well to trust him, and therefore <hi type="italic">got him up into the hold.</hi> It is dangerous venturing upon the mercy of a reconciled enemy. We read of those who believed in Christ, and yet he <hi type="italic">did not commit himself to them because he knew all men.</hi> Those that like David are innocent as doves must thus like him be <hi type="italic">wise as serpents.</hi>  <chapter eID="1Sam.24"/> <div eID="gen5784" type="x-p"/>

entries.8d18ed6560784cfcdcd95c5638a2b983ce24a157: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2756"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 24</title> <div sID="gen3766" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.1-1Sam.24.7">1Sa 24:1-7</reference>. David in a Cave at Engedi Cuts Off Saul's Skirt, but Spares His Life.<div eID="gen3766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3767" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2756"/><hi type="bold">2. Saul ... went ... to seek David ... upon the rocks of the wild goats--</hi>Nothing but the blind infatuation of fiendish rage could have led the king to pursue his outlawed son-in-law among those craggy and perpendicular precipices, where were inaccessible hiding places. The large force he took with him seemed to give him every prospect of success. But the overruling providence of God frustrated all his vigilance. <div eID="gen3767" type="x-p"/>
entries.75d41d099b52c579ffcfe293566e5d30b4ed7c5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2757"/><div sID="gen3768" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2757"/><hi type="bold">3. he came to the sheepcotes--</hi>most probably in the upper ridge of Wady Chareitun. There a large cave--I am quite disposed to say the cave--lies hardly five minutes to the east of the village ruin, on the south side of the wady. It is high upon the side of the calcareous rock, and it has undergone no change since David's time. The same narrow natural vaulting at the entrance; the same huge natural chamber in the rock, probably the place where Saul lay down to rest in the heat of the day; the same side vaults, too, where David and his men were concealed. There, accustomed to the obscurity of the cavern, they saw Saul enter, while, blinded by the glare of the light outside, he saw nothing of him whom he so bitterly persecuted. <div eID="gen3768" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3060818a02612e193279e4557ed5f094b9bf792: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2758"/><div sID="gen3769" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2758"/><hi type="bold">4-7. the men of David said ... Behold the day of which the Lord said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand--</hi>God had never made any promise of delivering Saul into David's hand; but, from the general and repeated promises of the kingdom to him, they concluded that the king's death was to be effected by taking advantage of some such opportunity as the present. David steadily opposed the urgent instigations of his followers to put an end to his and their troubles by the death of their persecutor (a revengeful heart would have followed their advice, but David rather wished to overcome evil with good, and heap coals of fire upon his head); he, however, cut off a fragment from the skirt of the royal robe. It is easy to imagine how this dialogue could be carried on and David's approach to the king's person could have been effected without arousing suspicion. The bustle and noise of Saul's military men and their beasts, the number of cells or divisions in these immense caverns (and some of them far interior) being enveloped in darkness, while every movement could be seen at the cave's mouth--the probability that the garment David cut from might have been a loose or upper cloak lying on the ground, and that Saul might have been asleep--these facts and presumptions will be sufficient to account for the incidents detailed.<div eID="gen3769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3770" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.8-1Sam.24.15">1Sa 24:8-15</reference>. He Urges Thereby His Innocency. <div eID="gen3770" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d76abf9657b3b13adffd67c86da9117c51895db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2759"/><div sID="gen3771" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2759"/><hi type="bold">8-15. David also arose ... and went out of the cave, and cried after Saul--</hi>The closeness of the precipitous cliffs, though divided by deep wadies, and the transparent purity of the air enable a person standing on one rock to hear distinctly the words uttered by a speaker standing on another (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.7">Jud 9:7</reference>). The expostulation of David, followed by the visible tokens he furnished of his cherishing no evil design against either the person or the government of the king, even when he had the monarch in his power, smote the heart of Saul in a moment and disarmed him of his fell purpose of revenge. He owned the justice of what David said, acknowledged his own guilt, and begged kindness to his house. He seems to have been naturally susceptible of strong, and, as in this instance, of good and grateful impressions. The improvement of his temper, indeed, was but transient--his language that of a man overwhelmed by the force of impetuous emotions and constrained to admire the conduct, and esteem the character, of one whom he hated and dreaded. But God overruled it for ensuring the present escape of David. Consider his language and behavior. This language--"a dead dog," "a flea," terms by which, like Eastern people, he strongly expressed a sense of his lowliness and the entire committal of his cause to Him who alone is the judge of human actions, and to whom vengeance belongs, his steady repulse of the vindictive counsels of his followers; the relentings of heart which he felt even for the apparent indignity he had done to the person of the Lord's anointed; and the respectful homage he paid the jealous tyrant who had set a price on his head--evince the magnanimity of a great and good man, and strikingly illustrate the spirit and energy of his prayer "when he was in the cave" (<reference osisRef="Ps.142.1">Psa 142:1</reference>). <chapter eID="1Sam.24"/>

entries.b5a02a9dd51acb3879386d3c3bd1a8cd4df0fdf4: <div eID="gen10383" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10384" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10385" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10385" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10384" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10386" type="x-p"/> Saul is informed that David is at En-gedi, and goes to seek him with three thousand men, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.1">1Sam 24:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.2">1Sam 24:2</reference>. He goes into a cave to repose, where David and his men lay hid; who, observing this, exhort David to take away his life: David refuses, and contents himself with privily cutting off Saul's skirt, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.3-1Sam.24.7">1Sam 24:3-7</reference>. When Saul departed, not knowing what was done, David called after him; showed him that his life had been in his power; expostulates strongly with him; and appeals to God, the Judge of his innocence, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.8-1Sam.24.15">1Sam 24:8-15</reference>. Saul confesses David's uprightness, acknowledges his obligation to him for sparing his life; and causes him to swear that, when he should come to the kingdom, he would not destroy his seed, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.17-1Sam.24.21">1Sam 24:17-21</reference>. Saul returns home, and David and his men stay in the hold, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.22">1Sam 24:22</reference>. <div eID="gen10386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10387" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10388" type="x-p"/> Saul was returned - It is very probable that it was only a small marauding party that had made an excursion in the Israelitish borders, and this invasion was soon suppressed.
entries.da19867a3da7a2dcfb1fe786564aad00f76b8888: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10389" type="x-p"/> Rocks of the wild goats - The original (צורי היעלים tsurey haiyeelim) is variously understood. The Vulgate makes a paraphrase: Super abruptissimas petras quae solis ibicibus perviae sunt; "On the most precipitous rocks over which the ibexes alone can travel." The Targum: the caverns of the rocks. The Septuagint make the original a proper name; for out of צרוי היעלים tsurey haiyeelim, they make Σαδδαιεμ Saddaiem, and in some copies Αειαμειν Aeiamein, which are evidently corruptions of the Hebrew.
entries.1fa4b7e0117b51dfbb2c1be0a1418a66ee2c1605: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10390" type="x-p"/> The sheep-cotes - Caves in the rocks, in which it is common, even to the present time, for shepherds and their flocks to lodge. According to Strabo there are caverns in Syria, one of which is capable of containing four thousand men: Ὡν ἑν και τετρακισχιλιους ανθρωπους δεξασθαι δυναμενον; lib. xvi. p. 1096. Edit. 1707. <div eID="gen10390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10391" type="x-p"/> Saul went in to cover his feet - Perhaps this phrase signifies exactly what the Vulgate has rendered it, ut purparet ventrem. The Septuagint, the Targum, and the Arabic understand it in the same way. It is likely that, when he had performed this act of necessity, he lay down to repose himself, and it was while he was asleep that David cut off the skirt of his robe. It is strange that Saul was not aware that there might be men lying in wait in such a place; and the rabbins have invented a most curious conceit to account for Saul's security: "God, foreseeing that Saul would come to this cave, caused a spider to weave her web over the mouth of it, which, when Saul perceived, he took for granted that no person had lately been there, and consequently he entered it without suspicion." This may be literally true; and we know that even a spider in the hand of God may be the instrument of a great salvation. This is a Jewish tradition, and one of the most elegant and instructive in their whole collection. <div eID="gen10391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10392" type="x-p"/> David and his men remained in the sides of the cave - This is no hyperbole; we have not only the authority of Strabo as above mentioned, but we have the authority of the most accurate travelers, to attest the fact of the vast capacity of caves in the East. <div eID="gen10392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10393" type="x-p"/> Dr. Pococke observes: "Beyond the valley (of Tekoa) there is a very large grotto, which the Arabs call El Maamah, a hiding place; the high rocks on each side of the valley are almost perpendicular, and the way to the grotto is by a terrace formed in the rock, which is very narrow. There are two entrances into it; we went by the farthest, which leads by a narrow passage into a large grotto, the rock being supported by great natural pillars; the top of it rises in several parts like domes; the grotto is perfectly dry. There is a tradition that the people of the country, to the number of thirty thousand, retired into this grotto to avoid a bad air. This place is so strong that one would imagine it to be one of the strong holds of En-gedi, to which David and his men fled from Saul; and possibly it may be that very cave in which he cut off Saul's skirt, for David and his men might with great ease lie hid there and not be seen by him." - Pococke's Travels, vol. ii., part 1, p. 41.
entries.d08763455cc52ca6d115ebc64bf542a34c83e6b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen10393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10394" type="x-p"/> And the men of David said - We know not to what promise of God the men of David refer; they perhaps meant no more than to say, "Behold, the Lord hath delivered thine enemy into thy land, now do to him as he wishes to do to thee." <div eID="gen10394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10395" type="x-p"/> Then David arose - Though I have a high opinion of the character of David, yet the circumstances of the case seem to indicate that he arose to take away the life of Saul, and that it was in reference to this that his heart smote him. It appears that he rose up immediately at the desire of his men to slay his inveterate enemy, and one whom he knew the Lord had rejected; but when about to do it he was prevented by the remonstrance of God in his conscience, and instead of cutting off his head, as he might have done, an act which the laws and usages of war would have justified, he contented himself with cutting off the skirt of his robe; and he did this only to show Saul how much he had been in his power.
entries.5a7c6e483de310ff7f09e8cca68efb123122b7c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10396" type="x-p"/> The Lord's anointed - However unworthily Saul was now acting, he had been appointed to his high office by God himself, and he could only be removed by the authority which placed him on the throne. Even David, who knew he was appointed to reign in his stead, and whose life Saul had often sought to destroy, did not conceive that he had any right to take away his life; and he grounds the reasons of his forbearance on this - He is my master, I am his subject. He is the Lord's anointed, and therefore sacred as to his person in the Lord's sight. It is an awful thing to kill a king, even the most untoward, when he has once been constitutionally appointed to the throne. No experiment of this kind has ever succeeded; the Lord abhors king killing. Had David taken away the life of Saul at this time, he would, in the sight of God, have been a murderer.
entries.f01133522256f8bb9bea481c7661d7a5e5412960: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen10396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10397" type="x-p"/> Suffered them not to rise against Saul - As he could restrain them, it was his duty to do so; had he connived at their killing him, David would have been the murderer. In praying for the king we call God the only Ruler of princes, for this simple reason, that their authority is the highest among men, and next to that of God himself; hence he alone is above them. We find this sentiment well expressed by an elegant poet: - <div eID="gen10397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10398" type="x-p"/> Regum timendorum in proprios greges, <div eID="gen10398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10399" type="x-p"/> Reges in ipsos imperium est Jovis. <div eID="gen10399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10400" type="x-p"/> Horace, Odar. lib. iii., Od. i., ver. 5. <div eID="gen10400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10401" type="x-p"/> Kings are supreme over their own subjects; <div eID="gen10401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10402" type="x-p"/> Jove is supreme over kings themselves.
entries.ffe7177aae257b9a097300762abbc3b17e8951e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen10402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10403" type="x-p"/> The Lord judge between me and thee - Appeals of this kind to God are the common refuge of the poor and oppressed people. So also among the Hindoos: God will judge between us. Mother Kalee will judge. Sometimes this springs from a consciousness of innocence, and sometimes from a desire of revenge.
entries.6a434c7c4d1d303c38038cb67cbc3afe2ca01594: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen10403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10404" type="x-p"/> Wickedness proceeded from the wicked - This proverb may be thus understood: He that does a wicked act, gives proof thereby that he is a wicked man. From him who is wicked, wickedness will proceed; he who is wicked will add one iniquity to another. Had I conspired to dethrone thee, I should have taken thy life when it was in my power, and thus added wickedness to wickedness.
entries.a3a10a324f1b26348077868a59c95c9db5c2d319: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen10404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10405" type="x-p"/> After a dead dog - A term used among the Hebrews to signify the most sovereign contempt; see <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.9">2Sam 16:9</reference>. One utterly incapable of making the least resistance against Saul, and the troops of Israel. The same idea is expressed in the term flea. The Targum properly expresses both thus: one who is weak, one who is contemptible.
entries.fb0d938074b2670459171c176d12db1e0820be39: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen10405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10406" type="x-p"/> The Lord therefore be judge - Let God determine who is guilty.
entries.0c0fa75878350f026dbbaed7f70fa846ea6c55ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen10406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10407" type="x-p"/> My son David? - David had called Saul his master, lord, and king. Saul accosts him here as his son, to show that he felt perfectly reconciled to him, and wished to receive him as formerly into his family.
entries.828ffaaf9527dba3feef52761ef0be868c9fc95f: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen10407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10408" type="x-p"/> If a man find his enemy, will he let him go well away? - Or rather, Will he send him in a good way? But Houbigant translates the whole clause thus: Si quis, inimicum suum reperiens, dimittit eum in viam bonam, redditur ei adomino sua merces; "If a man, finding his enemy, send him by a good way, the Lord will give him his reward." The words which are here put in italic, are not in the Hebrew text, but they are found, at least in the sense, in the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic, and seem necessary to complete the sense; therefore, adds Saul, the Lord will reward thee good for what thou hast done unto me.
entries.65cdaf766dcadbbcd34b0e561431ac77358be72f: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen10408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10409" type="x-p"/> I know well that thou shalt surely be king - Hebrew, Reigning, thou shalt reign. He knew this before; and yet he continued to pursue him with the most deadly hatred.
entries.6c45e7913c5472ebffbbe2da44fe4a75fe51b0d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen10409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10410" type="x-p"/> Swear now - Saul knew that an oath would bind David, though it was insufficient to bind himself; see <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.6">1Sam 19:6</reference>. He had sworn to his son Jonathan that David should not be slain; and yet sought by all means in his power to destroy him!
entries.c021ce92b2dc3c6673fac717ce2895ab69dc09ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen10410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10411" type="x-p"/> Saul went home - Confounded at a sense of his own baseness, and overwhelmed with a sense of David's generosity. <div eID="gen10411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10412" type="x-p"/> David and his men gat them up unto the hold - Went up to Mizpeh, according to the Syriac and Arabic. David could not trust Saul with his life; the utmost he could expect from him was that he should cease from persecuting him; but even this was too much to expect from a man of such a character as Saul. He was no longer under the Divine guidance; an evil spirit had full dominion over his soul. What God fills not, the devil will occupy.  <chapter eID="1Sam.24"/> <div eID="gen10412" type="x-p"/>

entries.ef6e8af514371cf69006f8d5ca0cf393be8dd8d9: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.1-1Sam.24.2">1Sa 24:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen4079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4080" type="x-p"/> When Saul had returned from his march against the Philistines, and was informed of this, he set out thither with three thousand picked men to search for David and his men in the wild-goat rocks. The expression “<hi type="italic">rocks of the wild goats</hi>” is probably not a proper name for some particular rocks, but a general term applied to the rocks of that locality on account of the number of wild goats and chamois that were to be found in all that region, as mountain goats are still (Rob. <hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. ii. p. 204).
entries.b03dbeb88050d61d86e18a4764ed903de96a9cb8: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.3">1Sa 24:3</reference> <div eID="gen4080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4081" type="x-p"/> When Saul came to the sheep-folds by the way, where there was a cave, he entered it to cover his feet, whilst David and his men sat behind in the cave. V. de Velde (<hi type="italic">R</hi>. ii. p. 74) supposes the place, where the sheep-folds by the roadside were, to have been the Wady <hi type="italic">Chareitun</hi>, on the south-west of the Frank mountain, and to the north-east of Tekoah, a very desolate and inaccessible valley. “Rocky, precipitous walls, which rise up one above another for many hundred feet, form the sides of this defile. Stone upon stone, and cliff above cliff, without any sign of being habitable, or of being capable of affording even a halting-place to anything but wild goats.” Near the ruins of the village of <hi type="italic">Chareitun</hi>, hardly five minutes’ walk to the east, there is a large cave or chamber in the rock, with a very narrow entrance entirely concealed by stones, and with many side vaults in which the deepest darkness reigns, at least to any one who has just entered the limestone vaults from the dazzling light of day. It may be argued in favour of the conjecture that this is the cave which Saul entered, and at the back of which David and his men were concealed, that this cave is on the road from Bethlehem to Ain-jidy, and one of the largest caves in that district, if not the largest of all, and that, according to Pococke (<hi type="italic">Beschr. des Morgenl</hi>. ii. p. 61), the Franks call it a labyrinth, the Arabs <hi type="italic">Elmaama</hi>, i.e., hiding-place, whilst the latter relate how at one time thirty thousand people hid themselves in it “to escape an evil wind,” in all probability the simoom. The only difficulty connected with this supposition is the distance from Ain-jidy, namely about four or five German miles (fifteen or twenty English), and the nearness of Tekoah, according to which it belongs to the desert of Tekoah rather than to that of Engedi. “<hi type="italic">To cover his feet</hi>” is a euphemism according to most of the ancient versions, as in Jdg 3:24, for performing the necessities of nature, as it is a custom in the East to cover the feet. It does not mean “to sleep,” as it is rendered in this passage in the <hi type="italic">Peschito</hi>, and also by Michaelis and others; for although what follows may seem to favour this, there is apparently no reason why any such euphemistic expression should have been chosen for sleep. “<hi type="italic">The sides of the cave</hi>:” i.e., the outermost or farthest sides.
entries.6886bba1be717c35bea4fd285f499250bb611230: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.4">1Sa 24:4</reference> <div eID="gen4081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4082" type="x-p"/> Then David’s men said to him, “<hi type="italic">See, this is the day of which Jehovah hath said to thee, Behold, I give thine enemy into thy hand, and do to him what seemeth good to thee</hi>.” Although these words might refer to some divine oracle which David had received through a prophet, Gad for example, what follows clearly shows that David had received no such oracle; and the meaning of his men was simply this, “Behold, to-day is the day when God is saying to thee:” that is to say, the speakers regarded the leadings of providence by which Saul had been brought into David’s power as a divine intimation to David himself to take this opportunity of slaying his deadly enemy, and called this intimation a word of Jehovah. David then rose, up, and cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak privily. Saul had probably laid the meil on one side, which rendered it possible for David to cut off a piece of it unobserved.
entries.d282b623effe36e5a782bff84bb2dd7d25975243: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.5">1Sa 24:5</reference> <div eID="gen4082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4083" type="x-p"/> But <hi type="italic">his heart smote him</hi> after he had done it; i.e., his conscience reproached him, because he regarded this as an injury done to the king himself.
entries.20825f74c03b2b3a96448ef9c80a26d391164dbe: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.6">1Sa 24:6</reference> <div eID="gen4083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4084" type="x-p"/> With all the greater firmness, therefore, did he repel the suggestions of his men: “<hi type="italic">Far be it to me from Jehovah</hi> (on Jehovah’s account: see at <reference osisRef="Josh.22.29">Jos 22:29</reference>), <hi type="italic">that</hi> (אם, a particle denoting an oath) <hi type="italic">I should do such a thing to my lord, the anointed of Jehovah, to stretch out my hand against him</hi>.” These words of David show clearly enough that no word of Jehovah had come to him to do as he liked with Saul.
entries.4df2d8feb7e2f0cacb68ac38b2134b1ca624be1f: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.7">1Sa 24:7</reference> <div eID="gen4084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4085" type="x-p"/> Thus he kept back his people with words (שׁסּע, <hi type="italic">verbis dilacere</hi>), and did not allow them to rise up against Saul, sc., to slay him.
entries.32ca494e676213ed88069a79f51c67668f8edc3b: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.8-1Sam.24.10">1Sa 24:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen4085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4086" type="x-p"/> But when Saul had gone out of the cave, David went out, and called, “<hi type="italic">My lord king</hi>,” that when the king looked round he might expostulate with him, with the deepest reverence, but yet with earnest words, that should sharpen his conscience as to the unfounded nature of his suspicion and the injustice of his persecution. “<hi type="italic">Why dost thou hearken to words of men, who say, Behold, David seeketh thy hurt? Behold, this day thine eyes have been that Jehovah hath given thee to-day into my hand in the cave, and they said</hi> (אמר, thought) <hi type="italic">to kill thee, and I spared thee</hi>:” <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. it (mine eye) spared thee (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.45.20">Gen 45:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.16">Deu 7:16</reference>, etc., which show that עיני is to be supplied).
entries.69ce55f85e1f16f480b215a882eb4a74c5ee3056: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.11">1Sa 24:11</reference> <div eID="gen4086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4087" type="x-p"/> To confirm what he said, he then showed him the lappet of his coat which he had cut off, and said, “<hi type="italic">My father, see</hi>.” In these words there is an expression of the childlike reverence and affection which David cherished towards the anointed of the Lord. “<hi type="italic">For that I cut off the lappet and did not kill thee, learn and see</hi> (from this) <hi type="italic">that</hi> (there is) <hi type="italic">not evil in my hand</hi> (i.e., that I do not go about for the purpose of injury and crime), <hi type="italic">and that I have not sinned against thee, as thou nevertheless layest wait for my soul to destroy it</hi>.”
entries.2259f644d1953c3e42a31795ce7edd1fa855b141: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.12-1Sam.24.13">1Sa 24:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen4087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4088" type="x-p"/> After he had proved to the king in this conclusive manner that he had no reason whatever for seeking his life, he invoked the Lord as judge between him and his adversary: “<hi type="italic">Jehovah will avenge me upon thee, but my hand will not be against thee. As the proverb of the ancients</hi> (הקּדמוני is used collectively) <hi type="italic">says, Evil proceedeth from the evil, but my hand shall not be upon thee</hi>.” The meaning is this: Only a wicked man could wish to avenge himself; I do not.
entries.e00aa1f04ddfc0689326955424277215a2528f67: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.14">1Sa 24:14</reference> <div eID="gen4088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4089" type="x-p"/> And even if he should wish to attack the king, he did not possess the power. This thought introduces <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.14">1Sa 24:14</reference> : “<hi type="italic">After whom is the king of Israel gone out? After whom dost thou pursue? A dead dog, a single flea</hi>.” By these similes David meant to describe himself as a perfectly harmless and insignificant man, of whom Saul had no occasion to be afraid, and whom the king of Israel ought to think it beneath his dignity to pursue. A dead dog cannot bite or hurt, and is an object about which a king ought not to trouble himself (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.8">2Sa 9:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.9">2Sa 16:9</reference>, where the idea of something contemptible is included). The point of comparison with a flea is the insignificance of such an animal (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.20">1Sa 26:20</reference>).
entries.cddc1426db80a72da73e8d4548d095d813a90cf2: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.15">1Sa 24:15</reference> <div eID="gen4089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4090" type="x-p"/> As Saul had therefore no good ground for persecuting David, the latter could very calmly commit his cause to the Lord God, that He might decide it as judge, and deliver him out of the hand of Saul: “<hi type="italic">Let Him look at it, and conduct my cause</hi>,” etc.
entries.84265a86e5525a141ad950dc63339509f7f5079f: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.16-1Sam.24.18">1Sa 24:16-18</reference> <div eID="gen4090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4091" type="x-p"/> These words made an impression upon Saul. David’s conduct went to his heart, so that he wept aloud, and confessed to him: “<hi type="italic">Thou art more righteous than I, for thou hast shown me good, and I</hi> (have shown) <hi type="italic">thee evil; and thou hast given me a proof of this to-day</hi>.”
entries.2cad2f132726522fe86bdb9d70fffb0580ba43dc: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.19">1Sa 24:19</reference> <div eID="gen4091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4092" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">If a man meet with his enemy, will he send him</hi> (let him go) <hi type="italic">in peace?</hi>” This sentence is to be regarded as a question, which requires a negative reply, and expresses the thought: When a man meets with an enemy, he does not generally let him escape without injury. But thou hast acted very differently towards me. This thought is easily supplied from the context, and what follows attaches itself to this: “<hi type="italic">The Lord repay thee good for what thou hast done to me this day</hi>.”
entries.eb507792ac0ba866a598e47e77124d1846ba4d9a: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.20-1Sam.24.21">1Sa 24:20-21</reference> <div eID="gen4092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4093" type="x-p"/> This wish was expressed in perfect sincerity. David’s behaviour towards him had conquered for the moment the evil demon of his heart, and completely altered his feelings. In this better state of mind he felt impelled even to give utterance to these words, “<hi type="italic">I know that thou wilt be king, and the sovereignty will have perpetuity in thy hand</hi>.” Saul could not prevent this conviction from forcing itself upon him, after his own rejection and the failure of all that he attempted against David; and it was this which drove him to persecute David whenever the evil spirit had the upper hand in his soul. But now that better feelings had arisen in his mind, he uttered it without envy, and merely asked David to promise on oath that he would not cut off his descendants after his death, and seek to exterminate his name from his father’s house. A name is exterminated when the whole of the descendants are destroyed, - a thing of frequent occurrence in the East in connection with a change of dynasties, and one which occurred again and again even in the kingdom of the ten tribes (vid., 1Ki 15:28., 1Sa 16:11.; 2 Kings 10).
entries.02933fc3764c65c450c5eced7268f175501145e4: <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.22">1Sa 24:22</reference> <div eID="gen4093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4094" type="x-p"/> When David had sworn this, Saul returned home. But David remained upon the mountain heights, because he did not regard the passing change in Saul’s feelings as likely to continue. המּצוּדה (translated “<hi type="italic">the hold</hi>”) is used here to denote the mountainous part of the desert of Judah. It is different in 1Sa 22:5.  <chapter eID="1Sam.24"/> <div eID="gen4094" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XXIV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>AND it came to pass, when Saul was returned from <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> after.</ns0:note> following the Philistines, that it was told him, saying, Behold, David is in the wilderness of En-gedi.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Then Saul took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel, and went to seek David and his men upon <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the face of, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> the rocks of the wild goats <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Which the wild Goats use to delight and climb into. These very Rocks are exceeding steep, and full of precipices, and dangerous to Travellers, as an eye-witness hath left upon Record. And yet <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> was so transported with Rage, as to venture himself and his Army here, that he might take <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid,</ns0:hi> who, as he thought, would judge himself safe, and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore be secure in such inaccessible places.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And he came to the sheep coats <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Which some think to have been Caves into which they used to drive their Sheep for shelter in tempestuous weather.</ns0:note> by the way, where <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> a cave, and * Saul went in to co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver his feet <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To ease his Belly, as this Phrase is thought to be used, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 3. 24. The reason whereof is, because the Eastern and some other Nations of old wore no Breeches, but loose and long Coats or Gowns, like those which Women with us wear; but shorter, whence their Feet and Legs were in a great part uncovered; and sometimes other parts, which al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so in Scripture are designed by the name of the Feet, (of which see on <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 49. 10. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 28. 57. 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 18. 27. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 7. 20.) were exposed to view. But when they went to per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />form this office of Nature, which obliged them first to lift up their Garments, they afterwards disposed them so decent<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, that all those parts might be covered and kept out of the sight of others. But possibly the words may have another meaning, and it is not to be despised, that those ancient and venerable Interpreters, the <ns0:hi>Syriack</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Arabick,</ns0:hi> Interpret this Place and Phrase quite otherwise, that <ns0:hi>Saul went in to sleep there:</ns0:hi> which was no uncouth thing to <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> who be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing a Military Man, used to sleep with his Soldiers upon the bare Ground, as he did <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 26. 7. And it is not improba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble that <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> being exceeding weary with his eager and al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />most incessant pursuit first of <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> then of the <ns0:hi>Philistines,</ns0:hi> and now of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> again, both needed and desired some sleep, God also disposing him thereunto, that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> might have this eminent occasion to demonstrate his integrity to <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> and to all <ns0:hi>Israel;</ns0:hi> and, the season possibly being hot, he might chuse to sleep in the Cave, for the benefit of the shade. But all the question is, how it may appear that this is the meaning of this Phrase, and what is the reason and ground of it? To which many things may be said. First, That this Phrase is but twice used in Scripture, as far as I remem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber, here, and <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 3. 24. and this sense may conveniently enough agree to both of them; nay, this sense may seem better to agree with that place, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 3. for that <ns0:hi>Summer Parlour,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Summer Chamber</ns0:hi> (for both seem to be the same place, and were apparently for the same use, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 24, 25.) seems to be a place far more convenient for sleeping, than for easing of Nature. And the Servants long stay and waiting for their Lord, seems to imply that they judged him gone to sleep (which might take up a considerable time), rather than to that other work which requires but a little time. See my Notes on <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 3. 24. Secondly, That there are many <ns0:hi>He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brew</ns0:hi> Phrases, which do confessedly signify several things, albeit, the reason of such significations be now utterly un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />known to us, though it was doubtless known to the ancient <ns0:hi>Hebrews.</ns0:hi> Nor need I instance in particulars, seeing it is so in all Languages, and particularly in the <ns0:hi>English</ns0:hi> Tongue at this day, in which the use of many Proverbs and Phrases is well understood, though the reason of them be now lost. Which if our modern <ns0:hi>Infidels,</ns0:hi> who scoff at some passages of Scripture, which they either do not, or will not under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand, would consider, they would lose much of their sport. Thirdly, Although there be not that clear and full proof of this sense which some may require (though indeed it cannot be reasonably expected in a thing so ancient, and in a Phrase of so concise and narrow a Language as the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> is, and in an expression so rarely used in Scripture), yet there are some intimations in Scripture which may seem to favour this Interpretation. For Persons composing themselves to sleep in this manner, are not onely Noted in the general to have been <ns0:hi>covered with a Mantle,</ns0:hi> as it is said of <ns0:hi>Sisera, Iudg.</ns0:hi> 4. 18, 19. but particularly they are said to have their <ns0:hi>Feet co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vered,</ns0:hi> as is expresly observed concerning <ns0:hi>Boaz</ns0:hi> when he lay down to sleep in the threshing-floor, <ns0:hi>Ruth</ns0:hi> 3. 4, 7. The rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son whereof may possibly be this, That when they lay down to sleep in their Garments, they were secured as to the other parts of their Body, onely their Feet were open and visible; and therefore it was convenient to cover their Feet; partly, to prevent the inconveniencies of cold, (for which reason we here take special care to cover our Feet in such cases); and partly, for decencies sake, lest their Garments being loose and large below, should be disordered, and so their Nakedness should appear, as it happened to <ns0:hi>Noah. Gen.</ns0:hi> 9. 21. Compare <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 20. 26. And therefore it cannot seem strange or forced, if in this place <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s covering of his Feet, design his composing himself to his rest. And if this be so, then the following difficulties of this History will appear to be plain and easie. For if <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> were fast asleep, which might easily be perceived by <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and his Men within; then it is not strange that <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> neither heard <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and his men talk<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of him, nor felt <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> when he came to cut off his lap.</ns0:note>: and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 57. title, and 142. title.</ns0:note> David and his men remained in the sides of the cave <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">For that there were vast Caves in those parts is affirmed not onely by <ns0:hi>Iosephus,</ns0:hi> but also by <ns0:hi>Heathen</ns0:hi> Authors; and <ns0:hi>Strabo</ns0:hi> in his <ns0:hi>16th</ns0:hi> Book writes of one which could receive Four thousand men.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:240" />4 And the men of David said unto him <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> How came it to pass that <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> did not hear the debates of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and his men? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> First, The greater noise of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Men and Horses just by the Caves mouth, might easily drown the lesser. Secondly, There were in these large and capacious Caves, several cells or parts, where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />of some were more inward and remote from the Caves mouth, in which they might freely converse and discourse, and yet neither be heard nor seen by <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> though they could easily see him, and observe all his postures and actions, because he was in the mouth of the Cave. 3. <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> might be asleep, as hath been discoursed.</ns0:note>, Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hold, the day of which the LORD said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand, that thou mayest do to him, as it shall seem good unto thee <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Not that either God said these words, or made any such particular promise, as some apprehend; but they put this construction upon those confessed and known promi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>es which God had made to him, of delivering him from all his Enemies, and carrying him through all hinderances and difficulties to the Throne and Kingdom: which promise they conceived put him under an Obligation of watching and taking all opportunities which God by his Providence should put into his hand for their accomplish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, whereof this was an eminent instance.</ns0:note>. Then David arose, and cut off the skirt of <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the robe which <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> Sauls.</ns0:note> Sauls robe privily <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Qu.</ns0:hi> How could <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> do thus, and <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> not perceive it? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> First, This might be some loose and upper Garment, which <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> might then lay at some distance from him, as we oft do on the same occasion. Secondly, In those vast Caves there were di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers particular Cells and Rooms which were distinct one from another, yet so as there were secret passages from one to another, as may be gathered from the relations of Historians and Travellers. At the mouth of one of these, <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> might lay his upper Garment: which <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> perceiving, and very well knowing all the Cells and Passages of that Cave, might go some secret way to it, and cut off a little part of it. Thirdly, The noise which <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s motion might be sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posed to make, was but small, and that he well knew would be perfectly drowned with the far greater noise of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />my, which lay at the mouth of the Cave. Fourthly, The Heroical Actions of great Men in Scripture are not to be measured by common rules. And as divers of the Prophets and Saints of old were in some of their Actions, so <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> might be in this, moved to it by a secret and Divine impulse, which also gave him confidence of Gods assistance therein, and of the Success of his Enterprize. Fifthly, This diffi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />culty doth perfectly vanish, if <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> was now asleep. And as no man can prove that he was not; so that he was, may seem probable from what is said on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And he said unto his men <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either, First, Before he cut off <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s lap. Or rather, Secondly, Afterwards, when he returned with <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s lap in his hand, and his Soldiers were enraged that he had not kil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led him.</ns0:note>, The LORD for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bid that I should do this thing <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Which you persuade me to do, even cut off <ns0:hi>Saul.</ns0:hi>

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Anointed by God to the Kingdom; by which Unction his Person was made Sacred and Inviolable, and is so to be ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />counted by me, and you, and all his Subjects. And as God onely Exalted him, and God onely could pronounce a Sen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tence of Deprivation of his Kingdom against him; so it be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />longs to God onely to execute his own Sentence, and actual<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly to Depose him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
