                        </ns0:gap> thou didst at any time fall into my hand.</ns0:note>, and I have not sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned against thee; yet thou huntest my soul to take it.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 The LORD judge <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> will judge.</ns0:note> between me and thee, and the LORD avenge me of thee <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>will avenge me of thee,</ns0:hi> to wit, if thou dost persist in thy injurious and cruel designs against me.</ns0:note>: but mine hand shall not be upon thee <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">I will not execute vengeance on thee, but will leave it wholly to God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 As saith the proverb of the ancients, Wick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />edness proceedeth from the wicked <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Wicked men will do wicked actions, among which this is one, to kill their Sovereign Lord and King; as <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> implied above, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. and more fully expresseth, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 26. 9. And therefore if I were so wicked and vile a Person as thy Courtiers represent me to thee, I should make no consci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence of laying wicked and violent hands upon thee, but should assassinate thee when I had opportunity. Which be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause I have now neglected and refused to do, though mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved to it by some of my wicked Soldiers; know therefore that I am not guilty of any wicked designs against thee, but am just and innocent towards thee. Or thus: wicked acti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons (such as they would have been if I had killed thee) pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceed onely from the wicked, of which number I am none, and therefore my hand shall not be upon thee.</ns0:note>: but mine hand shall not be upon thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 After whom is the king of Israel come out? after whom dost thou pursue? After a dead dog, after <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 26. 20.</ns0:note> a flea <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">After a worthless, contemptible, and impotent person, such as I am. Thou disparagest thy self in contending with such a Person; and even thy conquest of me will be inglori<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous and shameful.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 The LORD therefore be judge, and judge between me and thee, and see, and plead my cause, and <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> judge. 2 Sam. 18. 19.</ns0:note> deliver me out of thine hand.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 ¶ And it came to pass when David had made an end of speaking these words unto Saul, that Saul said, <ns0:hi>Is</ns0:hi> this thy voice, my son David <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">He knew his voice, though being at a great distance from him, he could not discern his face.</ns0:note>? And Saul lift up his voice, and wept <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Partly, from the sense of his sin against God, and of his wicked and base car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riage to <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> (for there are some such Temporary pas<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sions oft-times in Hypocrites and ungodly men) and princi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pally from the remembrance of so great and so late a danger as he had now escaped; which commonly produceth grief and tears; as 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 13. 36. Yet these may be tears of af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fection or tenderness (upon the sense of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s kindness) rather than of grief.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And he said to David, Thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> more righteous than I: for thou hast rewarded me good <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">For the Evil that I have designed and done to thee.</ns0:note>, whereas I have rewarded thee evil <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">For thy good will to me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And thou hast shewed this day how that thou hast dealt well with me: forasmuch as when the LORD had <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> shut up<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:note> delivered me into thine hand, thou killedst me not.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 For if a man find his enemy, will he let him go well away <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He will certainly destroy him. And therefore thou hast not dealt with me after the manner of men, but hast imitated the clemency of God in this act.</ns0:note>? wherefore the LORD re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward thee good, for that thou hast done unto me this day.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And now behold, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap 23. 17.</ns0:note> I know well <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Or, am convinced, not onely by the fame of <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi>'s Anointing thee, but by Gods singular Providence watching over thee; and by that good Spirit, and those Great and Princely Vertues wherewith God hath endowed thee.</ns0:note> that thou shalt be surely king, and that the kingdom of Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rael shall be established in thine hand.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 Swear now therefore unto me by the LORD, that thou wilt not cut off my seed after me <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">As Princes use to destroy their Competitors, and those that have any hopes of, or pretence to their Crown; and <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> had endeavoured to destroy <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> for the same reason, and therefore he feared a retaliation.</ns0:note>, and that thou wilt not destroy my name <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">To wit, by cutting off my Seed. So it is the same thing repeated in other words, as is usual in Scripture.</ns0:note> out of my fathers house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And David sware unto Saul <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Qu.</ns0:hi> How then could <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> destroy so many of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Sons, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 21. 8? <ns0:hi>Ans. David</ns0:hi> could bind himself by his Oaths, but he could not bind God, to whose good pleasure all Promises, Vows, Oaths, must in all reason be sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mitted; and that was done by Gods command, and God was well pleased with it, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 21. 14. Nor is it to be supposed that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> sware not to destroy any of them in case God should specially command it, or that should by miscarriage render themselves obnoxious to the Sword of Justice: but one<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly that he would not do it barely on his own private account, nor seek occasions of so doing.</ns0:note>: and Saul went home; but David and his men gat them up unto the hold <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To wit, of <ns0:hi>Engedi, v.</ns0:hi> 1. For having had so great and frequent experience of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s incon<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stancy, and malice, and perfidiousness, he would trust him no more.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
